definition: Predictable relationships between resources spent and performance obtained, which the archived sources invoke mostly to mark where the familiar ones stop applying. One derives a law inside RL training rather than pretraining: reward trades against policy entropy as R = -a*exp(H) + b, fitted across model families and predictive enough that coefficients from the first 36 steps extrapolate 200 steps ahead at under 1% RMSE, with the ceiling at zero entropy. The other observes that length generalization is often wholly independent of conventional scaling laws — models from 50M to 3B failed to extend 15-digit addition to 20 digits, and data past a threshold did not help. Both are cautions against reading a compute-loss curve as a capability curve.

evidence.note: Establishes that RL trades policy entropy for reward along a predictable exponential curve R = -a·exp(H) + b, derives that entropy change is driven by the covariance between action probability and advantage, and controls it by restricting updates to the highest-covariance tokens.
evidence.title: The Entropy Mechanism of Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Language Models

evidence.note: Proves that no computable length-generalization bound exists for transformers of depth two or beyond, and gives a matching exponential bound for the positive fragment that corresponds to fixed-precision transformers.
evidence.title: Length Generalization Bounds for Transformers

name: scaling laws
